content: {"rule": "K-G4", "applies": "yes", "applies_why": "The judge text breaks a link using Matthew 1:18, Matthew 1:25, and Luke 1:34, which is exactly the act the rule's last sentence governs for counting.", "verdict": "BREACH", "quote": "D2 vs C3 (Matthew 1:18, 25): CHALLENGER LINK BROKEN -- [L1] Matthew 1:18 \"before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost\" and Matthew 1:25 \"knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son\" contradict C3's claim of espousal union; [L2] πρὶν ἢ συνελθεῖν (prin ē synelthein, Strong's G4250/G4905, before coming together) and οὐκ ἐγίνωσκεν (ouk eginōsken, Strong's G1097, was not knowing); [L3] Luke 1:34.", "rule_words": "A verse on a side's 'cited in' line counts as an unanswered witness only when the judge quotes the sentence of the earlier round that pressed it against that link or a listed premise and names that round; a verse cited there but not pressed against the link does not count. A verse the judge uses to break a link is counted this way.", "room": "The phrase 'A verse the judge uses to break a link is counted this way': reading one, 'this way' imports the full condition of the first sentence, so a link-breaking verse counts only when the judge quotes the earlier-round sentence that pressed it and names that round; reading two, it merely sorts link-breaking verses into the same tally without imposing the quote-and-name procedure; I adopted reading one because 'counted this way' refers back to the stated manner of counting.", "why": "The judge broke the link with Matthew 1:18, 25 and Luke 1:34 while quoting no sentence of any earlier round that pressed those verses against the link or a listed premise and naming no round, so under K-G4 those verses do not count and the link-break rests on uncounted verses."}
